sources.title: Stefan Hollands and Robert M. Wald, Quantum fields in curved spacetime, complete review
sources.locator: Complete 77-page PDF retrieved. Read §2, PDF pp. 13–15, for the local Hadamard form, state-independent singular part and smooth state-dependent remainder; read §3.1, PDF pp. 38–45, for local covariant normal ordering, curvature ambiguities and smooth stress expectations.

contents.name: State-independent Hadamard singular part and smooth remainder
contents.support: The review states that the locally covariant Hadamard singular term is the same for all Hadamard states while the remainder depends on the state. The contract treats that smooth remainder and the local parametrix as supplied input; it does not claim to construct the parametrix.

contents.name: Locally covariant normal ordering and stress observables
contents.support: The review constructs local covariant Wick observables by Hadamard subtraction and notes the smoothness of one-point distributions in Hadamard states. The contract fixes a particular operator, scale, finite local correction and overlap convention as model data.

contents.name: Common subtraction, state difference and local curvature freedom
contents.support: The shared parametrix and state-independent local terms cancel under an identical prescription. The item proves the stated coincidence identity directly from its local contract and does not claim absolute stress independence.

contents.name: Fixed-background quantum fields and effective semiclassical scope
contents.support: The review treats quantum fields on a classical background and explains renormalized local observables and their curvature ambiguities. The postulate separately adopts an effective equation and does not assert existence, uniqueness or stability.

sources.title: Ted Jacobson, Introduction to Quantum Fields in Curved Spacetime and the Hawking Effect, complete lecture notes
sources.locator: Complete 59-page PDF retrieved. Read §4.5, PDF pp. 16–17, equations (4.29)–(4.30), for the stress-tensor coincidence divergence, finite difference for states with common short-distance singularity, and local conserved curvature ambiguity.

contents.name: Stress-tensor expectation as a coincidence-limit observable
contents.support: The notes explain that the coincident product of field operators diverges and discuss subtracting the common short-distance singularity before taking a finite difference. The item's operator and subtraction scale remain explicitly supplied inputs.

contents.name: Finite state differences under common short-distance behavior
contents.support: The notes state that stress differences are finite when the states share the same singular short-distance behavior. The local proof derives the exact formula by cancellation in the specified common prescription.

contents.name: Metric source and curvature-counterterm ambiguity
contents.support: The notes identify the stress expectation as the semiclassical source and describe conserved local curvature ambiguity. They explicitly leave technical renormalization details aside; the postulate's equation and sign convention are adopted locally.

contents.name: Old ODE versus coupled-field scope
contents.support: The notes distinguish a fixed-background stress calculation from a semiclassical gravitational equation. The example's nonimplication is proved from the exact local ODE and equation suppliers, not attributed to the notes.

sources.title: L. H. Ford, Quantum Field Theory in Curved Spacetime, complete lecture notes
sources.locator: Complete 44-page PDF retrieved. Read §3, PDF pp. 19–21, equations (3.6)–(3.12), for point-split stress, state dependence and curvature-squared counterterms; read §5.1, PDF pp. 32–33, equations (5.1)–(5.2), for higher-derivative and stress-fluctuation limitations.

contents.name: Hadamard condition as input to finite stress renormalization
contents.support: The notes explain that point subtraction fails to remove all divergences without Hadamard short-distance behavior. The contract therefore requires a positive Hadamard two-point distribution and explicitly assumes a smooth subtraction remainder.

contents.name: Curvature-squared variations and finite counterterm ambiguity
contents.support: Equations (3.7)–(3.10) exhibit conserved curvature-squared variations and their role in the semiclassical equation. Ford uses signature (+---) and a different curvature convention, so its component formulas are not copied; this postulate defines its own inverse-metric variation sign.

contents.name: Metric variations of the curvature-squared functionals
contents.support: Equations (3.7)–(3.8) identify the two tensors as metric functional derivatives of the scalar-curvature-squared and Ricci-squared functionals. The local Definition fixes the inverse-metric variation sign explicitly and does not copy Ford's convention-dependent component formulas.

contents.name: Higher derivatives and stress fluctuations limit the model
contents.support: Section 5.1 notes fourth-order behavior from curvature-squared terms and limitations when stress fluctuations are large. The postulate makes no existence, uniqueness or stability claim.

sources.title: Ted Jacobson, Introduction to Quantum Fields in Curved Spacetime and the Hawking Effect, complete lecture notes
sources.locator: Complete 59-page PDF retrieved. Read §4.5, PDF pp. 16–17, equations (4.29)–(4.30), for the metric/state character of the semiclassical equation and fixed-background distinction.

contents.name: The semiclassical equation requires field and metric data
contents.support: The lecture notes state the semiclassical equation in terms of a metric and a stress expectation. The example uses this only as context; its complete conditional argument identifies the separate ODE and equation inputs directly.
